title: Brightness of original-design Starlink satellites at 550 km

satellite.name: Starlink V1.0 (original design)
satellite.notes: Flat nadir-facing bus plus one solar array, no visor. Model: data/satellite_models/starlink_v1_0.json (design page M4).

phase_fit_linear.locator: Table 2, 'Phase angle' row (slope not significant; se 0.672)

flat_panel_fit.form: m1000 = b + mFP * (-2.5 log10(M N)); M, N = projections of the nadir-facing side toward the observer and toward the Sun (section 2, Figures 1-2)
flat_panel_fit.locator: section 4.3, equation 1; Table 2 'Flat-panel' row (7 sigma; se 0.654)

shell.locator: altitude: section 4; inclination not stated in the paper (Starlink shell 1 is 53.0 deg)

constraints.note: Selection limits are not stated. Magnitudes were reduced to 1000 km and phase angles computed by T. Molczan (section 3). The limits here are MEASURED (2026-10-22), not the paper's: the visual sites take the Sun window of Mallama et al. 2023b's own BlueWalker 3 visual rows (the same observers and method; Sun -24..-10 deg at the 2.5-97.5 percentiles) and the elevation limit measured for the VisorSat observers (>= 30 deg: mallama2021_visorsat.json's not-seen share). MMT-9 (its own entry) takes the 31 MMT tracks of STARLINK-1008 (V1.0, 2020-2025) replayed by SGP4: Sun 2.5-97.5 percentile -32.6..-10.7 deg; MMT follows high passes (median elevation of its 1.5-s bins 56 deg; track medians: median 61, 10th percentile 46), and >= 45 deg is the limit at which the sampler's median elevation (54) comes closest to MMT's while keeping its lower tail. A global window would not do: until 2026-10-22 SatBench assumed Sun -18..-6, elevation >= 20 for every site, and the 2020 Starlink models were fitted to that (M8); at MMT's real geometry they read ~0.9 mag too bright.
